questions.q: What is the overall goal of this capstone project, as framed in this lesson?
options: Build a trading strategy and backtest it against historical prices
Fit an ARMA model and a GARCH(1,1) model to each of five assets' returns, and estimate a one-factor covariance matrix across the universe compared to the sample covariance
Train a machine-learning classifier to predict which asset will perform best
Design a new options-pricing formula
questions.explain: The four concrete deliverables are: an ARMA fit with residual diagnostics per asset, a GARCH(1,1) fit per asset, a one-factor covariance matrix compared to the sample covariance, and a combined summary table -- using only tools from this course, not trading or ML.

questions.q: How is each asset's simulated return constructed in the universe setup?
options: As a random walk with no relationship to any other asset
As beta_i times a shared common factor, plus an asset-specific idiosyncratic shock, with both the factor and each idiosyncratic shock generated from their own GARCH(1,1) process
As the average of all five assets' historical prices
By downloading real historical price data for five real companies
questions.explain: The simulation follows r_i,t = beta_i * f_t + eps_i,t, where both the common factor f_t and each asset's idiosyncratic shock eps_i,t are generated from their own GARCH(1,1) process, giving the universe realistic volatility clustering.

questions.q: In the realized correlation matrix, why did QRBT (Quill Robotics) and HALC (Halcyon Software) show the highest pairwise correlation (0.344) in the whole matrix?
options: Because they are both in the technology sector by name only, which has no effect on correlation
Because they have the two highest factor betas (1.30 and 1.15), so they share the largest common exposure to the same underlying factor
Because they were simulated with the same random seed
Because their idiosyncratic shocks were set to zero
questions.explain: A one-factor model predicts that assets with the highest betas to the common factor will be most correlated with each other, since more of their return variance comes from the shared factor -- exactly the pattern QRBT and HALC showed.

questions.q: Why does fixing the random seed (np.random.seed(2024) plus specific per-asset seeds) matter for this capstone?
options: It makes the GARCH model converge faster
It makes the simulated universe exactly reproducible, so Lesson 34 can build directly on the same data and get the same numbers
It is required by the arch package to run at all
It removes the need for any volatility modeling
questions.explain: A fixed random seed means re-running the exact same simulation code produces identical returns every time, which is what lets Lesson 34 reuse this lesson's exact universe and get consistent, reproducible results.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about using Chapter 6's regime-switching models or any trading/ML techniques in this capstone?
options: The capstone requires fitting a full regime-switching model to every asset

The capstone stays within the ARMA/GARCH/factor-model toolkit from Chapters 1-7; regime-switching is mentioned only conceptually, and trading strategies or machine-learning models are explicitly out of scope
Machine learning models are required for the factor covariance estimate
Regime-switching models replace the need for GARCH entirely in this project
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly scopes the capstone to log returns, ARMA, GARCH, and a factor-model covariance -- noting regime-switching only as a conceptual aside -- and states that trading strategies, backtesting, and machine-learning models belong to other courses, not this one.
